chapter_title: Setting Up Your React dApp Environment
chapter_summary:
Embarking on dApp development with React and Web3.js begins with establishing a robust and organized development environment. The first crucial step is to create a new React project. While Create React App (CRA) has been a long-standing choice, modern development often favors Vite for its incredibly fast cold start and hot module reloading. For this course, we will utilize Vite to kickstart our React dApp, providing a streamlined and efficient development experience. To begin, open your terminal and execute the command `npm create vite@latest my-dapp -- --template react-ts` (if you prefer TypeScript) or `npm create vite@latest my-dapp -- --template react` (for JavaScript). This command scaffolds a new React project named `my-dapp` in a new directory, pre-configured with essential build tools. Navigate into your new project directory using `cd my-dapp` and install the initial dependencies with `npm install`.

Once your React project is set up, the next essential component is Web3.js. This library acts as our bridge to the Ethereum blockchain, allowing our React application to interact with smart contracts, manage accounts, and send transactions. To add Web3.js to your project, simply run `npm install web3` in your terminal. After installation, you'll be able to import and utilize the `Web3` object throughout your React components. It's good practice to verify the installation by adding a simple `console.log(Web3)` in your `App.tsx` or `App.jsx` file and checking your browser's developer console when the app is running (using `npm run dev`).

A critical aspect of dApp development, especially when dealing with blockchain networks, is the secure management of sensitive information. This includes API keys for Infura or Alchemy (if you're connecting to a remote node), contract addresses, and network IDs. Directly embedding these values in your source code is a significant security risk, as they would be exposed in the client-side bundle. Instead, we leverage environment variables. Vite, like CRA, supports `.env` files for this purpose. Create a file named `.env` in the root of your project. Inside, define your variables using the `VITE_` prefix for Vite to expose them to the client-side code, for example: `VITE_INFURA_PROJECT_ID=YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID` and `VITE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS=0x...`. In your React components, you can then access these variables via `import.meta.env.VITE_INFURA_PROJECT_ID`. Remember never to commit your `.env` file to version control (Git) by adding it to your `.gitignore`. This simple step is vital for preventing accidental exposure of sensitive credentials.

Beyond technical setup, a well-organized project structure is paramount for maintainability and scalability. For a React dApp, consider creating dedicated folders for different concerns. A `components` folder will house reusable UI elements, while a `hooks` folder can contain custom React hooks for blockchain-specific logic (e.g., `useWeb3`, `useContract`). A `utils` folder is useful for helper functions, such as formatting addresses or converting Wei to Ether. You might also want a `contracts` folder to store your smart contract ABIs (Application Binary Interfaces), which Web3.js needs to understand how to interact with your deployed contracts. For instance, you could have `src/components/`, `src/hooks/`, `src/utils/`, and `src/contracts/` directories. This modular approach helps keep your codebase clean, makes it easier to locate specific functionalities, and promotes code reusability, which is particularly beneficial as your dApp grows in complexity. Always prioritize clear naming conventions and consistent code formatting to ensure your project remains a joy to work with.

screens.title: Setting Up Your React dApp Environment
screens.subtitle: Fast project scaffolding, Web3.js integration, secure env management, and a scalable folder layout

narration.text: Today we'll set up a practical React dApp environment that is fast, maintainable, and secure. You will learn how to scaffold a React project using Vite for rapid iteration, add Web3. js so your frontend can talk to Ethereum, and keep secrets out of your client bundle with properly prefixed environment variables. We'll also sketch a pragmatic project layout with folders for components, hooks, utils, and contracts so your code stays organized as the dApp grows. For example, using Vite speeds up development feedback by shortening cold starts and making hot module reload feel immediate, which matters when you're iterating on blockchain interactions and UI. A common misconception is that any React starter is fine; in practice a faster tool like Vite improves productivity and reduces friction when testing transactions and contract calls. By the end of this lesson you will be able to scaffold the project, install Web3. js, create a. env with VITE_ variables, and place ABIs in a contracts folder. Keep an eye out for the verification steps that ensure Web3 is accessible and your environment variables are visible to the client without exposing secrets unintentionally. Ready to begin?

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson — practical setup goals

narration.text: These learning objectives focus your setup work so you can reliably build and test React dApps. First, you'll be able to initialize a modern React project using a build tool optimized for developer speed. This matters because faster reloads let you iterate on UI and blockchain logic without wasted time. Second, you'll install and configure Web3. js so the frontend can communicate with Ethereum nodes and contracts. Knowing how to import and verify Web3 is a basic requirement for any dApp frontend. Third, you'll understand environment variables with the VITE_ prefix, how to place them in a. env file, and why you must exclude that file from version control. This protects A P I keys and contract addresses from accidental exposure. Fourth, you'll structure your project with clear folders—components, hooks, utils, contracts—making the codebase easier to maintain and extend. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a competency milestone so you can confirm you've done the actual setup and verification. By the end, you'll have both the working repository and the reasoning behind each decision.

screens.title: Why choose Vite for a React dApp
screens.subtitle: Speed, HMR quality, and developer feedback loop

narration.text: When starting a React dApp you might wonder whether to use Create React App or Vite. The crucial differences are development speed and ergonomics. Vite provides a much faster cold start and near-instant hot module replacement by leveraging native browser ESM and a lean dev server. For dApp work, where you frequently change UI and re-run contract interactions, that speed saves minutes per iteration and reduces context switching. A common misconception is that build tools are interchangeable; in practice the faster reloads directly increase velocity for testing transactions and debugging asynchronous blockchain calls. Another point is configuration: Vite exposes environment variables that are intentionally prefixed; this ties directly into secure handling we will cover. An example: when you make UI changes to a component that calls a smart contract, Vite applies the update immediately without a full page reload, preserving app state and making it easier to re-run the same transaction scenario. Before you scaffold, confirm your Node version is compatible and that you have a package manager ready. The core insight is that tooling choice affects daily productivity, not just initial setup.

keyIdea.title: Tooling matters
keyIdea.text: Vite's faster dev loop materially improves dApp development velocity and debugging, especially when testing contract interactions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why choose Vite for a React dApp
Comparison: Vite vs CRA
Vite
Fast cold start, instant HMR, minimal dev server overhead. Better for frequent UI and contract testing.
Create React App
Stable and familiar, but slower rebuilds and larger dev server latency for iterative dApp work.
  • Vite preserves application state on updates, useful when reproducing blockchain call sequences.
  • Faster reloads mean you can iterate UI and contract integrations with less waiting.
  • Vite expects VITE_ prefix for exposed env variables, aligning with secure patterns.
Concrete example

Imagine you tweak a component that displays an account balance after a transaction. With Vite you change markup, save, and immediately test the transaction again without re-entering all steps. This reduces debugging time.

Common mistake

Assuming tooling is an afterthought. Slower tooling can hide stateful bugs and waste iteration time.

screens.title: Environment variables and the VITE_ prefix
screens.subtitle: Secure client-side configuration using Vite's rules

narration.text: Environment variables let you separate configuration and sensitive data from your source code. For client-side Vite projects, only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to the browser. This prevents accidental leakage of server-only secrets. When you create a. env file at your project root, define keys like VITE_INFURA_PROJECT_ID or VITE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS. Keep placeholders during development and never commit the file to version control. The. gitignore modification is a simple but essential step. A common misconception is that prefixing is optional; without the VITE_ prefix Vite will not expose variables to import. meta. env in the client bundle. Another pitfall is committing a. env file—this makes A P I keys public and can cause immediate security issues. Use placeholder values locally and manage real secrets through secure vaults or deployment systems in production. The visible example shows how to access variables at runtime via import. meta. env. This pattern keeps the build predictable and your keys safer. Environment variables and the VITE_ prefix means only vite_ prefixed variables are available to client code; keep .env out of version control to avoid leaking keys.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Create a .env and update .gitignore
screens.subtitle: Place placeholders for keys and prevent accidental commits

narration.text: Creating and protecting a. env file is a small step with large security benefits. In your project root, create a. env file and add VITE-prefixed placeholders for A P I keys and contract addresses. For example, add a placeholder for an Infura project ID and a deployed contract address. Then open your. gitignore and ensure. env is listed so the file does not get committed to your repository. This step prevents leaking keys to public repositories. A helpful habit is to include a. env. example file under version control that documents required keys but contains no secrets. That file serves as a template for teammates. A common pitfall is forgetting to add. env to. gitignore before a commit, which can expose keys immediately. After setting up. env, restart the dev server if necessary and verify import. meta. env contains the expected VITE_ keys. This workflow balances developer convenience with a minimal security posture appropriate for front-end dApps. screens.title: Organizing your React dApp folders
screens.subtitle: Practical layout: components, hooks, utils, and contracts

narration.text: A clear project structure reduces cognitive load and makes your dApp easier to extend. Start with src/components for presentational pieces and shared UI controls. Keep blockchain logic in src/hooks so hooks like useWeb3 or useContract encapsulate provider setup, account management, and contract instances. Use src/utils for helper functions: address formatting, unit conversion from Wei to Ether, and common error handlers. Store ABIs and optional deployed addresses in src/contracts so contract interfaces are easy to find and import into hooks. This separation encourages single responsibility and makes testing simpler. For example, a useContract hook can import an ABI from contracts and a VITE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS from import. meta. env, then return a contract instance for components to call. A common misconception is bundling Web3 logic into components; this leads to duplication and harder maintenance. Organize files with clear naming like useWeb3. js and TokenABI. json. As projects grow, consider grouping feature folders by domain, each containing components, hooks, and tests for that feature. Organizing your React dApp folders means keep ui, web3 hooks, utilities, and abis in separate folders to support reuse, testing, and clear ownership of responsibilities.. screens.title: Using ABI and contract address with Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Create a contract instance and call a read-only function

narration.text: To interact with a deployed contract you need two things: the contract address and its ABI. The ABI describes available functions and events so Web3. js can encode and decode calls correctly. In a typical pattern, store the ABI as a JSON file under src/contracts and read the deployed address from import. meta. env. VITE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS. A hook or initialization module can then create a contract instance by supplying a provider, the ABI, and the address. A practical example is a read-only balance or name call on a token contract. Importantly, the ABI is a structural description, not executable code, so it is safe to commit. A common misconception is treating ABI as secret; it is public by design. The code preview demonstrates creating a Web3 provider and contract instance, then calling a method and handling the returned promise. This pattern isolates contract interactions and makes them testable and reusable across components. Using ABI and contract address with Web3.js means store abis in src/contracts, read addresses from vite_ env vars, and create contract instances via web3 when you need to call functions.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Using ABI and contract address with Web3.js
How it works
  • ABI defines a contract's callable functions and event signatures.
  • Contract address tells Web3 which deployed instance to target.
  • Create a Web3 contract using new web3.eth.Contract(ABI, address) and call methods.
Misconception

The ABI is not secret. It is a public interface description required for interaction and safe to commit to the repository.

Code preview (visual)
<!-- src/hooks/useContract.js -->
import Web3 from 'web3'
import TokenABI from '../contracts/TokenABI.json'

export function createContract(){
  const web3 = new Web3(Web3.givenProvider || 'https://mainnet.example')
  const address = import.meta.env.VITE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS
  const contract = new web3.eth.Contract(TokenABI, address)
  return contract
}

// Usage: const contract = createContract(); contract.methods.name().call().then(...)
Key Takeaway

Keep ABIs in contracts/ and addresses in env vars; create contract instances in hooks for reuse.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common setup issues
screens.subtitle: Why your Web3 import or env variables might not behave as expected

narration.text: During setup you may encounter a few recurring problems. First, the Web3 import may appear undefined in the browser because node_modules were not installed correctly or the dev server needs to restart. Re-run the package manager install and restart the dev server to fix this. Second, environment variables not appearing usually means the VITE_ prefix was omitted or the. env file was placed in the wrong folder. Always place. env at the project root and prefix client-exposed keys with VITE_. Third, committing. env accidentally exposes keys; check your commit history and rotate keys if that happens. Fourth, mixing provider expectations can cause runtime errors—make sure to detect injected providers first and fall back to a remote RPC. A helpful debugging example is to log provider presence before creating contracts. These checks separate library availability from network connectivity and guide you to the next step: implementing reliable provider detection and error handling in hooks. Troubleshooting common setup issues means verify node_modules, restart the dev server, confirm vite_ prefixes and .env location, and detect providers before creating contract instances.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Troubleshooting common setup issues
Common issues and fixes
  • Missing Web3 object: run npm install and restart the dev server.
  • Env vars undefined: ensure VITE_ prefix and that .env lives at the project root. Restart if needed.
  • Accidental .env commit: remove from history and rotate keys; add .env to .gitignore immediately.
  • Provider errors: detect injected providers, then fall back to remote RPC; handle user-denied requests cleanly.
Check your console

Log Web3, import.meta.env, and provider presence. These logs tell you whether the issue is bundling, configuration, or runtime connectivity.

Warning

If env keys were leaked, rotate them. Treat leaked RPC keys as compromised credentials.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, Vite offers a fast development experience with quick cold starts and high-quality hot module reload, which speeds up UI and contract iteration. Second, Web3. js is the library that lets your frontend connect to Ethereum, but after installing it you still need to configure a provider and ABIs to perform contract calls. Third, environment variables must use the VITE_ prefix to be exposed to the client; never commit real. env files to source control. Fourth, organize your code with components for UI, hooks for Web3 logic, utils for helpers, and contracts for ABI files. These choices reduce technical debt and make collaboration easier. As you continue, remember that these foundations are about reproducibility, security, and developer productivity. Keep your. env files private, store ABIs in a clear location, and favor hooks for provider and contract setup so your UI remains simple and testable.

narration.text: Keep three compact reminders in mind as you build. First, choose fast tooling like Vite to speed iterations and preserve state during hot reloads. Second, protect your keys: use VITE_ prefixed variables in. env and never commit that file; provide a. env. example as documentation. Third, separate concerns by placing UI in components, Web3 logic in hooks, helpers in utils, and ABIs in contracts. Together these habits reduce errors, make debugging simpler, and let you focus on building features that interact with smart contracts. As you move forward, treat setup as part of your development process: revisit environment handling and folder organization when adding new integrations or teams to your project.
